title: Redis, Caching & Rate Limiting
primer: Redis is for hot paths: cache-aside, counters, locks, and rate limits — not a second source of truth. Design for stampede, hot keys, and TTL freshness, and always plan what happens when Redis dies so PostgreSQL does not avalanche. Atomicity comes from INCR, MULTI/EXEC, or Lua — not from get-modify-set in application code.

questions.question: When should an API use Redis instead of querying PostgreSQL directly?
questions.first30s: When the same read is hot, tolerates slight staleness, and DB cost or latency dominates — not for every query by default.
modelAnswer: Use Redis for high-QPS reads with stable keys (session, product config, permission bitsets, feed fragments) where TTL/staleness is acceptable.
Keep PostgreSQL as source of truth for durable, transactional, strongly consistent writes and complex queries.
Cache after measuring: p95 DB time, QPS, and hit-rate potential — don't cache unique one-off queries.
Prefer cache-aside with explicit invalidation/TTL; avoid dual-writing critical money state only to Redis.
Also use Redis for ephemeral coordination: rate limits, locks, short-lived idempotency keys.
questions.sayIt: Redis for hot, slightly stale reads and coordination. Postgres for truth and transactions — I cache when the hit rate and latency win are proven.
questions.nestNote: Inject a cache port in Nest providers so services don't scatter raw Redis calls.
traps: Caching everything including low-hit unique keys
Treating Redis as the system of record for balances
No TTL and no invalidation plan
followUps: What hit rate justifies the complexity?

questions.question: Redis goes down during peak traffic. How should the application degrade?
questions.first30s: Fail fast on Redis with timeouts, then either serve stale/local data, skip non-critical cache, or shed load — never unbounded synchronous fallback to the DB.
modelAnswer: Short connect/command timeouts and circuit breaker around Redis so threads don't pile up.
Decide policy per feature: fail-open (skip cache, hit DB with cap) vs fail-closed (rate limiter denies / feature disables).
Protect PostgreSQL with concurrency limits, cached-in-process soft state, and load shedding on non-critical endpoints.
Optionally serve last-known-good from local/memory cache with longer TTL during outage.
Alert on Redis health and DB QPS spike; rehearse the degradation in game days.
questions.sayIt: Redis down: timeout fast, degrade by feature, and cap DB fallback — an uncapped fallback is an outage multiplier.
questions.nestNote: Separate Redis modules (cache vs rate-limit) so one policy doesn't blindly apply to both.
traps: Infinite retries to Redis on the request path
Failing open on rate limiting (abuse flood)
No circuit breaker → thread pool exhaustion
followUps: Should rate limiting fail open or closed?
How do you warm the cache after Redis recovers?

questions.question: How would you implement cache-aside for a read-heavy endpoint?
questions.first30s: Read Redis by key; on miss load Postgres, SET with TTL, return. Invalidate or overwrite on writes. Add stampede protection for hot keys.
modelAnswer: Key design: versioned, namespaced keys including tenant/id (e.g. prod:user:{id}:profile:v2).
Read path: GET → hit return; miss → DB → SET EX ttl → return.
Write path: update DB then DEL/SET the key (invalidate or write-through); accept brief race windows consciously.
Add jittered TTLs; singleflight/lock on miss for popular keys.
Metrics: hit rate, miss latency, DB load on misses; negative-cache empty results carefully.
questions.sayIt: Cache-aside: GET, miss to DB, SET with TTL; invalidate on write; singleflight so misses don't herd.
questions.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>API: GET
  API->>Redis: GET key
  alt hit
    Redis-->>API: value
  else miss
    API->>Postgres: SELECT
    API->>Redis: SET EX
  end
  API-->>Client: response
questions.code:
val = redis.get(key)
if val is None:
    val = db.fetch()
    redis.setex(key, ttl, serialize(val))
return val
questions.nestNote: Serialize JSON/msgpack consistently; include schema version in the key or payload.
traps: Caching without TTL
Updating DB but forgetting invalidation
Caching personalized responses under a shared key
followUps: Write-through vs cache-aside trade-offs?
How do you handle null / not-found caching?

questions.question: How would you handle stale cache data after a PostgreSQL update?
questions.first30s: Invalidate or overwrite the cache key in the same request after a successful DB commit — and accept TTL as a backstop for missed invalidations.
modelAnswer: After COMMIT, DELETE the affected keys (or SET the fresh value). Prefer explicit invalidation for correctness-sensitive data.
Keep TTLs short enough that missed invalidations self-heal; use key versioning when payload shape changes.
For multi-key entities, maintain a key inventory or hierarchical tags (careful: tag systems can be expensive).
If using replicas, beware read-your-writes: invalidate then read primary, or version stamp the payload.
Measure stale-read complaints; for strong freshness, skip cache on that path.
questions.sayIt: Commit first, then invalidate or SET the new value. TTL is the safety net for races and missed deletes.
questions.code:
async with db.transaction():
    await db.update(...)
await redis.delete(cache_key)  # after commit
questions.nestNote: Hook invalidation in the repository/unit-of-work after commit callbacks.
traps: Invalidating before commit (rollback leaves hole or race)
Infinite TTL with best-effort invalidation only
Forgetting secondary keys derived from the entity
followUps: How do you invalidate lists that contain the entity?
Would CDC/outbox-driven invalidation help?

questions.question: What is a cache stampede scenario and how would you prevent it?
questions.first30s: Stampede is many requests missing the same key at once and all hitting the DB. Prevent with singleflight, a lock, probabilistic early refresh, or serving stale while one refreshes.
modelAnswer: Scenario: hot key TTL expires (or cold start) → N concurrent misses → N identical DB queries.
Singleflight / request coalescing in-process: one loader, others wait.
Distributed: SET lock key NX EX; winner loads DB and fills cache; losers wait/retry or serve stale.
Probabilistic early expiration / soft TTL: refresh before hard expiry under load.
Jitter TTLs so many keys don't expire in the same second; monitor miss spikes.
questions.sayIt: Stampede = thundering herd on miss. One refresher via lock or singleflight; others wait or get stale.
questions.code:
ok = redis.set(f'lock:{key}', '1', nx=True, ex=5)
if ok:
    val = db.fetch()
    redis.setex(key, ttl, val)
    redis.delete(f'lock:{key}')
else:
    # wait briefly and GET again, or serve stale
    ...
questions.nestNote: In multi-instance Node, in-process singleflight alone is not enough — need Redis NX lock or similar.
traps: Only jittering TTL but not locking the hottest key
Lock without TTL (deadlock if refresher dies)
Retry loops without backoff while lock held
followUps: How does 'serve stale-while-revalidate' work with Redis?
What's the difference between stampede and hot-key CPU saturation?

questions.question: A popular Redis key becomes a hot key. How would you handle it?
questions.first30s: A hot key saturates one shard/CPU. I'd add a local in-process cache, or split the keyspace across N sibling keys and aggregate.
modelAnswer: Confirm with Redis hot-key metrics / proxy stats / latency on one cluster node.
L1 local cache (with short TTL) on app instances to absorb read QPS.
Shard the key: value replicated on key:0..N-1 randomly read; for counters, INCR random shard and SUM on read (approximate or exact merge).
Reconsider storing a huge value; compress or split fields.
If Cluster mode, note hash-tag pinning can concentrate load — avoid accidental hot hash slots.
questions.sayIt: Hot keys need L1 caching or key sharding — scaling the cluster alone won't help if one key owns one slot.
traps: Adding Redis nodes without splitting the key
Hash tags that force many hot keys onto one slot
Global locks on the hot key for every read

questions.question: How would you choose TTLs for data with different freshness requirements?
questions.first30s: TTL follows the business freshness SLO: seconds for volatile counters, minutes for profiles, hours for rare config — always with jitter and an invalidation story for critical updates.
modelAnswer: Classify data: strict freshness (skip cache or TTL seconds + invalidate), eventual (minutes), static (hours/days).
Set TTL slightly above typical update interval; use explicit DEL on writes for stricter paths.
Add random jitter (±10–20%) to prevent synchronized expiry stampedes.
Negative caching: short TTL for misses to avoid DB hammering on hot 404s.
Review TTLs with hit-rate and stale-read metrics; document per-key-family policy.
questions.sayIt: TTL is a freshness SLA. Short + invalidate for volatile data, longer for static, jitter everything, short negative cache for misses.
traps: One global TTL for all keys
No jitter on millions of keys with the same expiry
Eternal keys for data that does change
followUps: How do you expire keys that are too large to scan with KEYS?

questions.question: How would you design a distributed per-user and per-IP rate limiter using Redis?
questions.first30s: I'd use Redis atomic counters or a sliding-window ZSET, with separate keys for userId and IP, evaluated in the gateway/middleware before expensive work.
modelAnswer: Fixed window: INCR key; on first INCR set EXPIRE windowSeconds; reject when count > limit (simple, bursty at boundaries).
Sliding window: ZADD timestamps, ZREMRANGEBYSCORE old, ZCARD — more accurate; often via Lua for atomicity.
Keys: rl:user:{id}:{bucket}, rl:ip:{ip}:{bucket}; apply both limits (AND).
Fail-closed or fail-open policy when Redis is down — usually fail-closed for auth abuse paths.
Return standard headers (remaining/reset); shard hot IP keys if under attack; observe top offenders.
questions.sayIt: Per-user and per-IP keys with atomic INCR or sliding-window Lua, checked early in the middleware, with an explicit Redis-down policy.
questions.code:
-- simplified fixed window
local c = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
if c == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end
return c
questions.nestNote: Apply in Nest guard/middleware before controllers; don't rely only on per-instance memory limits.
traps: Non-atomic get/set rate counters
Only IP limits (NAT) or only user limits (pre-auth flood)
Failing open on login endpoints during Redis outage
followUps: Token bucket vs sliding window?
How do you rate-limit at API gateway vs app?

questions.question: Two application instances update the same Redis-based counter concurrently. How would you make the operation safe?
questions.first30s: Use Redis atomic primitives — INCR/INCRBY or a Lua script — never GET, add in process, SET.
modelAnswer: Prefer INCR/INCRBY/DECR for single counters; they are atomic across clients.
For multi-key or conditional updates, use Lua (EVAL) or MULTI/EXEC transactions.
Avoid read-modify-write in app code across instances — classic race.
If absolute accuracy across Redis failover matters, understand Redis persistence/replication limits or keep durable counters in Postgres.
Test with concurrent workers; monitor for script errors and key type mismatches.
questions.sayIt: INCR or Lua — not get-add-set. Redis atomic ops are the concurrency control.
questions.code:
redis.incrby('metrics:signup', 1)
# or Lua for compare-and-swap style logic
traps: GET + SET across instances
Using MULTI without understanding WATCH for optimistic cases
Storing counters only in Redis when finance needs auditability
followUps: When do you need Lua vs a single INCR?
How does Redis Cluster affect multi-key Lua?

questions.question: How would you prevent a cache outage from causing a database avalanche?
questions.first30s: Treat Redis failure as expected: circuit-break, admit only a bounded number of DB fallbacks, shed non-critical traffic, and keep a small local stale cache.
modelAnswer: Timeouts + circuit breaker on Redis so the app fails fast instead of wedging.
Bulkhead: limit concurrent DB queries on cache-miss/fallback paths (semaphore).
Serve stale L1 content where safe; disable expensive list endpoints under degradation mode.
Load shed / adaptive concurrency at the edge when DB saturation rises.
Game-day: kill Redis in staging and verify DB QPS stays within ceiling; alert on fallback rate.
questions.sayIt: Avalanche prevention is bounded fallback: breakers, semaphores, stale serve, and shedding — not 'just query Postgres.'
questions.nestNote: Feature-flag 'degraded_mode' to flip caches off intentionally during incidents with known DB headroom.
traps: Silent unlimited DB fallback
Retry storms compounding load
No distinction between critical and optional reads
followUps: How do you size the fallback semaphore?
